title: Post-Tonal Theory
intro: Much twentieth-century music abandons the tonal centre. Post-tonal theory describes it with pitch classes, integers and sets: a toolkit for finding the patterns that hold atonal music together.

blocks.text: A pitch class is all the notes with one name in every octave, with enharmonics equal: every C, B♯ and D𝄫 is pitch class 0. The twelve pitch classes are numbered C = 0, C♯/D♭ = 1, D = 2 … B = 11, with T (10) and E (11) sometimes used as single symbols. Arithmetic is mod 12: 11 + 3 = 2.

items: Pitch interval: semitones between two actual pitches, with direction (+7 for C4 up to G4).
Pitch-class interval: (b − a) mod 12, from 0 to 11.
Interval class: the smaller of a pc interval and its inversion, 0 to 6. A fifth (7) and a fourth (5) are both interval class 5.

blocks.text: A set is an unordered collection of pitch classes, written in brackets: a C major triad is [0,4,7]. Two operations relate sets:

items: Transposition Tn: add n to every member. T2 of [0,4,7] is [2,6,9], a D major triad.
Inversion In: subtract every member from n, I0 = negation. I0 of [0,4,7] is [0,8,5], which reordered is [0,5,8]: an F minor triad. Inversion turns major triads into minor ones.

blocks.text: A set class (Forte's classification) groups every set related by transposition or inversion. All major and minor triads are one set class, 3-11, with prime form [0,3,7]. The prime form is the most compact ordering, starting on 0.

items: Put the pitch classes in ascending order within an octave and pick the rotation that spans the smallest interval from first to last (the normal order); if tied, the one packed most tightly to the left.
Transpose so the first element is 0.
Do the same for the inversion; the prime form is whichever of the two is more packed to the left.

blocks.text: The interval-class vector counts how many of each interval class (1 to 6) a set contains. For [0,3,7]: intervals 3, 7→ic5, 4 give ⟨001110⟩: one ic3, one ic4, one ic5. Sets with the same vector but different set classes are Z-related (Forte's 'Z' sets), such as 4-Z15 [0,1,4,6] and 4-Z29 [0,1,3,7], both ⟨111111⟩, the all-interval tetrachords.

widget.title: Webern-like sets: hear 3-11, 3-3 and the all-interval tetrachord

blocks.text: Play a set and its inversion with mirror hands: the right hand plays the set upward from a note, the left hand plays it downward from the same note, using the same fingers. The keyboard's symmetry around D (and around G♯/A♭) makes the inversion visible: D–F♯–A in the right hand mirrors to D–B♭–G in the left.

items: Twelve-Tone Technique (#/arts/music-theory/post-tonal/twelve-tone): rows, the row matrix and serialism.

blocks.title: Prime form
blocks.text: Find the prime form of {E, G, G♯} (pcs 4, 7, 8).
solution: Normal order: rotations 4-7-8 (span 4), 7-8-4 (span 9), 8-4-7 (span 11). Best: [4,7,8]. Transposed to 0: [0,3,4].
Inversion of [0,3,4]: [0,9,8] → normal order [8,9,0] → [0,1,4]. Compare [0,3,4] and [0,1,4]: [0,1,4] is more packed to the left.

blocks.text: Sources: Forte, A. (1973). The Structure of Atonal Music. Yale University Press; Straus, J. N. (2016). Introduction to Post-Tonal Theory, 4th ed. W. W. Norton; Rahn, J. (1980). Basic Atonal Theory. Longman; Tymoczko, D. (2011). A Geometry of Music. Oxford University Press.
